Nurses at a hospital in Berlin are on strike, protesting against understaffing and poor working conditions. Among them is 26-year-old Schirin. This is her story.

Schirin moved to Berlin two years ago after training as a nurse in Bremen, and now works at Charite.

Nurses at Charite have carried out a series of strikes over what they say is dangerous understaffing that puts patients at risk. The strikes come alongside protests in Germany in recent weeks, while metalworkers at companies across the country have also walked off the job demanding higher pay.

Schirin says the problems go beyond hospitals. She says the government is cutting money from schools, universities and public services, and that high rents are a big problem in Germany. She describes a huge gap between rich and poor.

Al Jazeera’s Tanya Noury says the US and Iran ended a two-month lull in fighting this week with tit-for-tat strikes. She says US firepower in the region is among its highest levels since 2003. 

David Des Roches, a former director of Arabian Peninsula Affairs in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, says the forces are there to enforce the blockade and project power from sea. He says a return to war is inevitable, as Iran will not accept being strangled indefinitely, or Trump may decide to resume major air strikes. He calls Israel the wild card, and says it is not sustainable for the US to keep this deployment for long.

description:
A French court has sentenced three police officers to five years in prison over the beating of a black music producer in 2020, recognising the assault as racist. The case has reignited debate over police violence and accountability in France.

Zecler’s lawyer, Serge Money, says the judgement shows that even a police officer lies, and that a person who says police made him suffer can be credible.

The verdict comes after two months of protests in France, with some saying the police response has been heavy-handed.

Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler reports from Paris.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
The United States is imposing a new rule to further restrict access to its advanced AI chips worldwide. Officials say it closes a loophole that allowed China to circumvent US restrictions.

The Commerce Department says the rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from renting computing power through data centres in other countries that have legally bought advanced chips. 

Al Jazeera’s Matthew Torres says the rule would require data centres in Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Brazil to apply for a special licence to buy the chips from American companies such as Nvidia. 

Beijing has condemned the rule, accusing the US of economic coercion. Analysts call the controls a major step but question how effectively they can be enforced.

Al Jazeera’s Matthew Torres reports from Washington, DC.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
An abandoned colonial courthouse in Senegal’s capital, Dakar, has found a new purpose as a space for artistic expression.

The Dakar Biennale brings together African and diaspora artists to explore themes of vulnerability, resilience, and identity. Beyond celebrating creativity, the exhibition is reclaiming a painful past, aiming to give African artists a platform to tell their own stories.

From sculptures and paintings to digital art, artists are exploring the theme of anti-fragility, using their vulnerability as a force of creation. 

Al Jazeera’s Nicolas Haque reports from Dakar.
